title: IISc Professor Critiques IIT Curriculum in AI Era
summary: IISc Bengaluru professor questions IIT students studying ancient shastras while AI reshapes technical education. Debate highlights India's STEM priorities.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- IISc Bengaluru professor publicly questions IIT students studying ancient shastras amid AI's rapid advancement in technical fields
- Critique sparks debate over curriculum relevance in India's top engineering institutions during technological transformation
- Discussion highlights tension between traditional knowledge systems and cutting-edge AI skills in Indian higher education


An IISc Bengaluru professor has ignited debate within India's academic community by questioning whether IIT students should study ancient shastras during an era defined by artificial intelligence breakthroughs. The critique, delivered November 2, 2026, challenges curriculum priorities at India's most prestigious engineering institutions as AI reshapes technical education globally.


## The Core Criticism


The professor's remarks target what they perceive as a misalignment between traditional knowledge systems and the urgent skills demands of modern AI-driven industries. While IIT institutions have historically balanced humanities with engineering, the unnamed faculty member argues that ancient text studies consume time better spent on machine learning, neural networks, and computational methods that define contemporary technical careers.


This intervention comes as Indian tech graduates face intense global competition in AI roles. Major employers increasingly prioritize candidates with practical AI implementation experience over broad liberal arts foundations, raising questions about optimal curriculum design for 2026 graduates.


## Release Date and Context


Officially released on November 2, 2026, the professor's statement arrives during India's ongoing national education policy review. Multiple IIT campuses have recently expanded their humanities requirements, arguing that ethical frameworks and historical context strengthen engineers' decision-making capabilities, particularly in AI development where bias and societal impact remain critical concerns.


## IIT Curriculum Structure


Current IIT programs typically require students to complete foundation courses across multiple disciplines, including some exposure to Indian knowledge traditions. Proponents defend this approach as producing well-rounded engineers capable of navigating complex socio-technical challenges. Critics counter that every hour spent on non-technical subjects delays mastery of rapidly evolving AI frameworks and tools.


- Most IIT branches mandate 10-15 credits in humanities and social sciences
- Shastra courses typically represent optional electives, not core requirements
- AI-focused specializations have grown from 12% to 34% of IIT enrollments since 2024


## Industry Perspectives


Indian AI startups and multinational research labs have expressed mixed reactions to the debate. Some hiring managers emphasize that cultural literacy helps engineers build products for diverse user populations, while others prioritize candidates demonstrating hands-on experience with transformer architectures and reinforcement learning systems. The tension reflects broader uncertainty about how technical education should adapt as AI capabilities accelerate.


## What This Means


The IISc professor's critique surfaces fundamental questions about Indian engineering education at a pivotal moment. As AI transforms every sector from healthcare to agriculture, institutions must balance timeless analytical skills with cutting-edge technical training. Whether IITs adjust their curricula in response, or defend interdisciplinary approaches as essential for ethical AI development, will shape India's competitiveness in global technology markets for years to come. The outcome may influence how technical universities worldwide navigate similar tensions between specialization and breadth.
